messages.subject: wrong mixing
parts:
I'm trying to fit a model with categorical distribution sampling. I have it wokring on JAGS, but couldn't fit it in Stan.
Any suggestions about what's going wrong? Am I incrementing log posterior in the right way? Is it even possible to fit this model in Stan? 
 It goes like this:

JAGS code: model{
  for (i in 1:m){
     k[i] ~ dbin(theta,n)
  }   
  theta ~ dbeta(1,1)
  n ~ dcat(p[])
  for (i in 1:nmax){
    p[i] <- 1/nmax
  }}   
Description of example:
There are five helpers distributing a bundle of surveys to houses. It is known that each bundle contained the same number of surveys, n, but the number itself is not known. The only available relevant information is that the maximum bundle is Nmax = 500, and so n must be between 1 and Nmax. (https://webfiles.uci.edu/mdlee/BB_Free.pdf, page 51)


My RStan code:
model ="
data { 
  int nmax; 
  int m;
  int k[m]; 
  int n[nmax];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
  simplex[nmax] mix;
} 
model {
  real ps[nmax];
  theta ~ beta(1, 1);  
  
  for (i in 1:m) {
    for (j in 1:nmax) {
      ps[j] <- log(mix[j]) + binomial_log(k[i], n[j], theta);
    }
    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);
  }
}"

k <- c(16, 18, 22, 25, 27)
m <- length(k)
n <- seq(max(k),500,by=1)
nmax <- length(n)

data <- list(k=k, m=m, nmax=nmax, n=n) # to be passed on to Stan

sa=sample(1:10,nmax,replace=T)
sa=sa/sum(sa)
sb=sample(1:10,nmax,replace=T)
sb=sa/sum(sa)
sc=sample(1:10,nmax,replace=T)
sc=sa/sum(sa)

myinits <- list(
  list(theta=runif(1), mix=sa),
  list(theta=runif(1), mix=sb),
  list(theta=runif(1), mix=sc))

# parameters to be monitored:  
parameters <- c("theta")

samples <- stan(model_code=model,   
                data=data, 
                init=myinits,  
#                pars=parameters,
                iter=1000, 
                chains=3, 
                thin=1)

RESULTS
JAGS results:















Stan results:
Mixing is flat. Theta varies from 0 to 0.1


Thank you,

Martin Smira

OK, I now understand the model after waking up and reading the
reference you linked. I rewrote the model and R code
to place more of the computation inside Stan.

You'll see if you look at the traceplots that theta converges
almost instantly [use: traceplot(fit,"theta") in R].

If you wanted, you could use the generated quantities block
and theta to generate samples for n. Stan only dumps out
the unnormalized log probabilities, which I've coded up as
a transformed parameter.

Instead, I would recommend doing inference directly in expectation with what Stan
produces --- Rao-Blackwell says it should be more efficient. So I added code
to do the normalized dump of probablity of n given data, as well as posterior mean.
Posterior mode's also easy to calculate or view by inspection (it's 73). So

Oh, this is great. Thank you Bob for the effort.

The results really match. 

I have a few questions: 
  In my model, I was incrementing log posterior like this (see below). How does it actually differs from yours? It differs only in the one 1:m loop. 

MY
for (i in 1:m) {

for (j in nmin:nmax) {
      lp_for_n[j] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k[i], n[j], theta);
    }
    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);
  }  
YOURS
  for (n in nmin:nmax)
    lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k,n,theta);
}
  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);

  How would you sample n in qenerated quantities using theta? I couldn't solve it. 

Thank you.

Martin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] wrong mixing
parts:
On 9/5/13 11:48 AM, Martin ï¿½mï¿½ra wrote:
> Oh, this is great. Thank you Bob for the effort.

I like nice problems like this --- it's more fun than
Sudoku :-)

> The results really match.

It is rather amazing that so many seemingly different
sampling algorithms get the same results.

> I have a few questions:
> In my model, I was incrementing log posterior like this (see below). How does it actually differs from yours? It
> differs only in the one 1:m loop.
>

> *MY*
> / for (i in 1:m) {/
> / for (j in nmin:nmax) {/
> / lp_for_n[j] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k[i], n[j], theta);/
> / }/
> / lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);/
> }
> *YOURS*
> / for (n in nmin:nmax)/
> / lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k,n,theta);/
> /}/
> / lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);/

It's just the order of the loops. I found it easier to think about
computing the marginal for each n rather than looping the other way.
It also let me use vectorization. The inner loop in my code could be
expanded to:

lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- log(1.0 / ntot);
for (i in 1:m)

lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] + binomial_log(k[i],n,theta);

I also just used arithmetic rather than computing an n[j] to lookup.
Arithmetic's usually faster than memory lookup, and I find it easier
to understand.

> How would you sample /n/ in qenerated quantities using theta? I couldn't solve it.

generated quantities {
int n; // you could bound this, but I'm too lazy to go back and figure it out
n <- categorical_rng(theta);
}

This generates n from p(n|theta) = Categorical(n|theta). You'll get one
random draw per iteration based on theta in that iteration, so that
p(theta,n|data) has the right joint distribution in the data, because
theta is generated from p(theta|data).

Note that you need to declare theta as a vector here --- it's the
only parameter categorical_rng accepts.

- Bob

Yes, it's an interesting example, but tricky too. 

I've found out that the results match just in theta, not in n, which you computed in R. The distribution of n is completely different. In your results n seems to be normaly distributed around the mean. But the BUGS results are skewed to the right, with possible probabilities also for high values of n. 

I have solved at last. Here is the code if you're interested. Instead of taking the mean of lp_for_n, I was working with with whole vector of 474 values, standardized it and used for sampling. Now the results match very nicely. See attached pdf.

lp_for_n.samples <- fit.samples$lp_for_n;
theta.samples <- fit.samples$theta
prob_n = matrix(rep(NA,474*4000),nrow=4000,ncol=474)
for (n in 1:4000) {
  max_log_prob_n_propto[n] <- max(lp_for_n.samples[n,])
  prob_n[n,] = exp(lp_for_n.samples[n,] - max_log_prob_n_propto[n]);
}
n = c()
  for (i in 1:4000){
    n[i]<-sample(27:500,1,prob=prob_n[i,],replace=T)

But can you help me with implementing the sampling of n to Stan please? You said that I could use n <-categorical_rng(theta). But I don't get it. Theta is just scalar. On what bases it could be transformed to vector of n size? Did you mean to use lp_for_n instead? After transforming it first. 
Thank you Bob.

Martin

> size? Did you mean to use lp_for_n instead? After transforming it first.

I'm not surprised I botched the normalization in R. You shouldn't
need to sample, though --- you can just compute the distribution once you
have theta. It looks just like what you did in R and then sampled.

And you do the same thing to sample in the generated quantities block
in Stan. You need to define the prob_n vector as above and then use

n <- categorical_rng(prob_n)

to sample. For the categorical distribution, you'll need
to normalize, or you'll get a runtime error.

If you define prob_n as a transformed parameter, you can also use
it to define lp__ and it will also get printed. Or you can define
it again in the generated quantities block as a local variable.

- Bob
